titel: Calculemus: An Introduction to the Philosophical Predecessors of Artificial Intelligence
note: Author note: This essay serves as a stand-alone introduction to the digital research apparatus *Calculemus: Philosophical Predecessors of AI* and as introductory text for the site itself. The site’s editorial matter is released under CC BY 4.0; source code under the MIT license; editions and derived data under CC0 1.0. Repository: https://github.com/pantaleonfassbender-coder/Philosophical-predecessors-of-AI

paras: In the summer of 1955, four researchers proposed a workshop at Dartmouth College on the conjecture “that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it” (McCarthy et al., 1955/2006, p. 12). The Dartmouth proposal gave the field of artificial intelligence its name and is routinely cited as its founding document. The conjecture itself, however, was not new. Three centuries earlier, Thomas Hobbes had opened *Leviathan* by asking why we may not say “that all Automata (Engines that move themselves by springs and wheeles as doth a watch) have an artificiall life,” and had defined reason as “nothing but Reckoning” (Hobbes, 1651, Introduction; pt. I, ch. V). The debate about thinking machines is older than the machines—older, indeed, than the electric telegraph. What the twentieth century contributed was hardware and a name; the questions, the programme, and the principal objections were already on the table.

*Calculemus: Philosophical Predecessors of AI* (Fassbender, 2026) is a digital research apparatus built on that observation. It gathers, in careful public-domain editions, the primary texts in which the idea of mechanical reason was first proposed, formalized, built, and contested—and, in a fourth line, narrated: sixteen modules reaching from the golden handmaids of the *Iliad* and the letter-wheels of the *Sefer Yetzirah* to Karel Čapek’s *R.U.R.* of 1920, with their core in the six centuries from Ramon Llull’s combinatorial wheels of 1308 to Charles Sanders Peirce’s survey of the logical machines of 1887. Every paragraph in the corpus carries a stable, citable number; a concordance searches all texts at once; and a term atlas maps the shared vocabulary of the corpus. The site takes its name from Leibniz’s celebrated proposal that disputants should one day settle their arguments by computation: *Calculemus*—let us calculate (Leibniz, 1875–1890, Vol. 7).

The deep history of artificial intelligence has been written more than once—as narrative (McCorduck, 2004), as philosophical analysis (Haugeland, 1985; Pratt, 1987), and as a history of logic running “from Leibniz to Turing” (Davis, 2000). What has been harder to come by is the evidence itself: the primary texts are scattered across rare printings, subscription archives, and editions of very unequal reliability, and they are rarely citable to the paragraph. The premise of this apparatus is that the prehistory of AI deserves what classical scholarship has always given its sources—exact citation, stated editorial method, and the standing possibility of checking a claim against the very sentence that grounds it. This essay introduces the corpus: the four lines along which it is organized, the argument that runs through them, the reason the collection ends where it does, and the way the apparatus is meant to be used.

abschnitte.titel: Reason as Reckoning: The Logic Line
paras: The first line of the corpus—its spine—is the direct intellectual ancestry of symbolic artificial intelligence: the succession of thinkers for whom reasoning could be treated as a rule-governed manipulation of symbols. Its deepest root is medieval. In the *Ars brevis* of 1308, Ramon Llull described an art of finding truth built from an alphabet of nine letters, a set of figures, and—most remarkably—three concentric rotating wheels whose alignments generate 252 combinatorial “chambers,” each a candidate proposition to be examined (Llull, 1308/1617). Llull’s aims were theological and missionary, not computational, and his art is not an algorithm in any modern sense (Bonner, 2007). But the device embodies an idea with a long future: that the space of possible assertions can be generated mechanically, by exhaustive combination, before any of them is judged. Leibniz named Llull’s art expressly as an inspiration of his own *ars combinatoria*, which is why the corpus opens here.

The founding sentence of the computational theory of mind, however, belongs to Hobbes. In chapter V of *Leviathan*, reason is defined as “nothing but Reckoning (that is, Adding and Subtracting) of the Consequences of generall names agreed upon” (Hobbes, 1651, pt. I, ch. V). The Introduction had already framed the state itself as an “Artificiall Man” and life as “but a motion of Limbs,” placing the artificial squarely within the natural order. Haugeland (1985) accordingly treated Hobbes as the “grandfather” of artificial intelligence, and the judgment is difficult to resist: if thinking is computation over symbols, then the question of whether a machine could think becomes an engineering question rather than a metaphysical one. The corpus presents the Introduction and the first five chapters of Part I in the spelling of the 1651 printing, so that the reader meets the sentence as the seventeenth century did.

Leibniz turned Hobbes’s aphorism into a research programme—and acknowledged the debt in writing: his early *De arte combinatoria* of 1666 cites Hobbes’s doctrine that all work of the mind is computation (Leibniz, 1875–1890). The programme had two parts: a *characteristica universalis*, a symbolic language in which concepts would be represented by characters as perspicuously as numbers are by numerals, and a *calculus ratiocinator*, a set of rules for operating on those characters so that valid reasoning becomes correct calculation. In the fragments collected in the corpus, Leibniz draws the famous consequence: when disputes arise, two philosophers need quarrel no more than two accountants—it will suffice to take pens in hand and say to each other, *Calculemus* (Leibniz, 1875–1890, Vol. 7). The anthology also includes his *Explication de l’arithmétique binaire* of 1703, which established the arithmetic of 0 and 1 in which all modern computation is conducted, and the *Monadology*, whose seventeenth section supplies—remarkably, from the same pen—the first great objection to machine minds, discussed below. Davis (2000) has traced how directly the road runs from this programme to modern computability theory.

The nineteenth century supplied what Leibniz lacked: a working algebra of thought. Boole’s *An Investigation of the Laws of Thought* (1854) opens with the declaration that its design is “to investigate the fundamental laws of those operations of the mind by which reasoning is performed,” and to express them “in the symbolical language of a Calculus.” The corpus carries the philosophical frame of the book—the preface, the first three chapters, and the closing chapter XXII—in which logic becomes literally a matter of equations. That this was more than a formal curiosity became clear three generations later, when Shannon (1938) showed that Boole’s algebra describes the behavior of relay and switching circuits: the bridge over which logic walked into hardware.

The line culminates in Frege. The *Begriffsschrift* of 1879 constructed the first complete formal system of quantified logic—a “formula language of pure thought” in which inference proceeds by explicit syntactic rule (Frege, 1879); van Heijenoort (1967) opened his source book of mathematical logic with it, judging it perhaps the most important single work ever written in the field. The *Grundlagen der Arithmetik* (Frege, 1884) then argued that arithmetic itself is further-developed logic, and “Über Sinn und Bedeutung” (Frege, 1892) drew the distinction between the sense of an expression and its reference on which formal semantics, and with it the knowledge-representation tradition of AI, still stands. With Frege, the logic line reaches the threshold of the twentieth century: everything Turing needed from logic existed by 1892, though no one yet knew what it would be needed for.

abschnitte.titel: Where the Idea Met Brass: The Machine Line
paras: The second line of the corpus follows the idea into matter. It begins with Pascal, whose arithmetical machine of the 1640s was the first calculating device to pass from design into use, and whose *Pensées* contain the first recorded philosophical reaction to computing machinery. The fragment is double-edged, and the corpus quotes it whole: “The arithmetical machine produces effects which approach nearer to thought than all the actions of animals. But it does nothing which would enable us to attribute will to it, as to the animals” (Pascal, 1670/1904, fragment 340, Brunschvicg numbering). In two sentences Pascal states both halves of the modern debate: the machine’s performance genuinely resembles thought, and something—here named will—still seems to be missing. Four further fragments in the module, including the “thinking reed” and the observation that “we are as much automaton as mind,” frame thought as the mark of human dignity precisely while conceding the mechanical in us.

Two centuries later, Ada Lovelace supplied the machine line with both its greatest promise and its most durable objection. Her 1843 translation of Menabrea’s sketch of Babbage’s Analytical Engine, expanded by her own Notes to nearly three times its length, contains in Note G the celebrated verdict: “The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to *originate* any thing. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform” (Lovelace, 1843, Note G). The same Notes, it should be said, articulate more clearly than Babbage ever did what a general-purpose programmable machine would be—including the insight that it might operate on symbols other than numbers, music among them. Turing (1950) took the objection seriously enough to answer it by name, as “Lady Lovelace’s objection,” and the contemporary debate over generative systems re-argues it under new vocabulary: whether a system trained to do what we ordered can be said to originate anything is, once again, a live question.

William Stanley Jevons built the machine. His “On the Mechanical Performance of Logical Inference,” read to the Royal Society in 1870, describes the “logical piano”: a device of keys, levers, and pallets that, given premises in Boole’s algebra (as reformed by Jevons), displays their valid conclusions—the first machine in history to perform logical inference (Jevons, 1870; Gardner, 1958). The corpus’s selection preserves what is philosophically most valuable in the memoir: not only the mechanism but Jevons’s sober self-assessment that the machine’s chief importance is “of a purely theoretical kind,” a caution against precisely the inflation that accompanies reasoning machines in every century.

The machine line closes with Peirce (1887), a working logician’s review of the reasoning machines of his day—Jevons’s piano and Allan Marquand’s improvement of it—published in the first volume of the *American Journal of Psychology*. Peirce asks exactly the question the corpus is built around: how much of the business of thinking a machine could possibly be made to perform, and what part of it must remain to the living mind. His answer—that every reasoning machine is bounded by its want of originality and initiative, and that precisely this gives machines their value, by showing how far reasoning is a mechanical process at all—may serve as the corpus’s epigraph for the machine line.

A prehistory that collected only the enthusiasts would be propaganda. The third line of the corpus gathers the classic arguments that machine intelligence is impossible—arguments that today’s debate keeps rediscovering, usually without knowing their age. The oldest and most precise is Descartes’s. In Part V of the *Discours de la méthode*, Descartes grants that a machine might utter words, and even words occasioned by bodily changes, but denies that it could ever “reply appropriately to everything that may be said in its presence, as even the lowest type of man can do”; and he adds a second test, generality—reason as a “universal instrument” against the special-purpose dispositions of any mechanism (Descartes, 1637, pt. V). Read today, the passage is startling: it is the Turing test stated in the negative, three centuries in advance, with unrestricted linguistic competence proposed as the criterion that separates minds from machines. Whether large language models have met Descartes’s criterion, or merely its appearance, is the most Cartesian question of the present decade.

The second counter-voice comes from inside the logic line itself. In section 17 of the *Monadology*, Leibniz asks the reader to imagine a machine whose construction produces thought, enlarged until one could walk into it as into a mill: inside one would find “only pieces working upon one another, and never anything by which to explain a perception” (Leibniz, 1714/1898, §17). The mill argument—that no arrangement of mechanical parts, however intricate, seems to account for experience—is the ancestor of every argument from consciousness against machine minds, down to the present dispute over whether anything is “like” anything for a computational system.

The third voice answers the first two by dissolving the contrast. La Mettrie’s *L’Homme Machine* of 1747 takes Descartes’s mechanical account of animals and extends it, deliberately and scandalously, to man: the human being does not merely resemble a machine—he is one, “a machine that winds its own springs” (La Mettrie, 1747/1912). If materialism about the mind is true, then the question is no longer whether matter can think—it demonstrably does—but only how. Two centuries later, McCulloch and Pitts (1943) gave that wager its formal turn, modeling the activity of nervous tissue as a logical calculus; the line from *L’Homme Machine* to the neural-network tradition is indirect but real. Within the corpus, La Mettrie also occasions a small editorial finding: the standard 1912 English translation silently omits seven paragraphs of the French text—bowdlerization, not variance—and the site’s edition restores them, marked in place.

The line’s last voice, a century younger than the others, reverses the direction of the whole dispute. Ernst Kapp’s *Grundlinien einer Philosophie der Technik* of 1877—the book that coined the phrase “philosophy of technology”—argues that the question had been posed the wrong way round: man is not a machine; the machine is an unconscious projection of the human organism (Kapp, 1877). Tools prolong the hand, the telegraph maps the nervous system, and in each case the maker recognizes his own bodily order in the artifact only afterward—technology as the detour by which humanity attains self-knowledge. Against La Mettrie, Kapp insists that whoever truly believes in his own personhood “will never confuse himself with a technical contrivance”; against naïve mechanism, that the resemblance of organism and machine runs from the living body outward, not back. When the present debate describes large language models as projections of human language returned to their makers, it speaks—mostly without knowing it—Kapp’s dialect.

Set beside these, Lovelace’s Note G and Pascal’s rider on will show that the machine line and the counter-voices are not opposing camps but one continuing conversation: nearly every builder in this corpus also stated, with precision, what the built thing could not do.

abschnitte.titel: The Animated Word: The Narrative Line
paras: The fourth line of the corpus does not argue; it narrates. Long before reason was defined as reckoning, the made servant was alive in story, and the stories hold a knowledge the treatises cannot: what it is to create by language, to command a literal executor, to lose control of a process one has started, and to face a made thing that cannot answer. The line opens at the oldest site of the Western imagination of automation. In Book XVIII of the *Iliad*, Hephaestus’ tripods roll “of their own selves”—the Greek word is αὐτόματοι—to the assembly of the gods, and his golden handmaids work “like real young women, with sense and reason, voice also and strength” (Homer, 1898 trans.). Aristotle cites that very passage when, in the *Politics*, he states the argument from automation once and for all: if every instrument could accomplish its work on command or by anticipating it, “master-builders would need no assistants, and masters no slaves” (Aristotle, Politics I 4, 1253b). The counterfactual he thought impossible is the condition the machine line begins, two millennia later, to build.

The golem tradition tells the making itself. In the corpus’s anthology the word appears first in the Psalms—*golmi*, “my unformed mass” (Ps 139:16)—and the Talmud supplies the two founding scenes. Rava creates a man and sends him to Rabbi Zeira, who addresses him, receives no answer, and returns him to dust: the language test as narrative, a millennium before Descartes stated it as argument (Sanhedrin 65b). And two sages create a calf for the Sabbath by study of the *Sefer Yetzirah* (Sanhedrin 65b)—the Book of Formation whose letter-combinatorics, twenty-two letters “fixed in a wheel” of two hundred and thirty-one gates, are the same combinatorial imagination that resurfaces, turned toward logic, in Llull’s rotating figures (Sefer Yetzirah 2:4–5; on the tradition, Scholem, 1965; Idel, 1990). The legend reached modern literature through a single paragraph: Jacob Grimm’s notice of 1808 in the *Zeitung für Einsiedler*, given here from the original printing, in which the servant of clay is animated by an inscription—*emet*, truth—and destroyed by the effacement of one letter—*met*, dead—and in which one master, having let his golem grow past his reach, is crushed under the collapsing clay (Grimm, 1808). Creation by letters, control by a stop-word, and the maker buried beneath his servant: the narrative line’s whole argument is already in it. The later Prague legend of Rabbi Loew, a nineteenth- and twentieth-century construction, is documented on the method page but deliberately not carried as text.

Goethe’s *Der Zauberlehrling* of 1797 compresses the control problem into fourteen stanzas: an animated servant that executes its instruction literally and tirelessly; a countermeasure—the axe—that doubles the process it was meant to stop; and, at the center, the confession on which a whole later literature hangs: *Hab ich doch das Wort vergessen*—the stop-command is forgotten, and only the returning master holds the word that revokes (Goethe, 1798). Norbert Wiener chose precisely this ballad, together with the golem, as the emblem of the danger of automatic machines whose purpose, once set, we can no longer revise (Wiener, 1950, 1964); the AI-safety literature still calls the failure mode the sorcerer’s-apprentice problem.

The line ends where myth hands over to industry, in the city where the golem legend had settled. Karel Čapek’s *R.U.R.* of 1920 re-derives the made servant from cost: young Rossum “threw out everything that does not serve work directly. In doing so he threw out the man and made the Robot”—mechanically more perfect than we are, astonishingly intelligent, “but they have no soul” (Čapek, 1920). The play gave every language the word robot, from *robota*, compulsory labour, and its ending sets against all manufacture the one thing that cannot be manufactured: the first pair, “who have invented love.” Sixteen years later Turing defined the abstract machine. The narrative line stops at its own side of the same threshold; what lies beyond it—Wiener’s *God and Golem, Inc.* (1964), where cybernetics itself takes up these very stories—is named in the site’s coda rather than carried.

The corpus ends, deliberately, where the modern reader expects it to begin. Turing’s two epochal papers—“On Computable Numbers” (Turing, 1937), which defined the abstract machine on which the theory of computation rests, and “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” (Turing, 1950), which proposed the imitation game and answered the classic objections, Lovelace’s among them—remain under copyright in the United States, as do the classic mid-century papers of the field’s founding generation. A corpus whose entire method depends on carrying its texts in full, in the public domain, therefore cannot include them; it can only point at them. The boundary of the site is thus a rights fact, not an editorial judgment of importance (Fassbender, 2026). But the constraint has a virtue: it forces attention onto the generation *before* the machines began to answer back, and it makes visible how much of the twentieth-century debate was already in place before the twentieth century. The reader who comes to Turing (1950) after this corpus will find its central moves—the language criterion, the objection from originality, the argument from consciousness, the computational wager about matter—already three centuries old, and will read the paper the way its own author did: as an intervention in a very long argument (cf. Dyson, 2012; McCorduck, 2004).

abschnitte.titel: The Apparatus: Editions, Citation, and Limits
paras: *Calculemus* is a static website with no build step, no accounts, and no tracking, and a single optional server function—the citation-bound dialogue described below; its data files, extraction tooling, and editorial method are open in the accompanying repository (Fassbender, 2026). Each of the sixteen shipped modules is a reading edition prepared from a stated source: trusted transcriptions (Project Gutenberg, Wikisource, the Deutsches Textarchiv, the Sefaria exports of the public-domain Hebrew and Aramaic texts) where they exist, and hand-emended optical character recognition of the original printings—Taylor’s *Scientific Memoirs* for Lovelace, the 1617 Zetzner printing for Llull, the 1879 Halle printing for Frege’s preface, the 1877 Braunschweig printing for Kapp and the 1808 *Zeitung für Einsiedler* for Grimm, in both cases verified against the page images of the scans—where they do not. Works written in Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Aramaic, French, German, or Czech are presented bilingually. Where a public-domain English translation exists (Latta’s Monadology, Veitch’s Descartes, Bussey’s La Mettrie, Trotter’s Pascal, Butler’s Homer, Ellis’s Aristotle, Bowring’s Zauberlehrling), it is used and named; where none exists—notably for Frege, for Leibniz’s computational texts, for Kapp, for the Hebrew sources and for Čapek—the site supplies working translations of its own, marked as such, carrying no scholarly authority, and dedicated to the public domain. The rule for scholarly use is stated on every relevant page: cite the original.

The organizing discipline of the apparatus is the citation grid. Every paragraph of every text carries a stable identifier in the form native to its work: Boole by his own article numbers, Jevons by his; the *Monadology* by section, Pascal by Brunschvicg number, Hobbes by chapter and editorial paragraph, with the marginal notes of the 1651 printing preserved as labels. Where a numbering is the site’s own—because the original printing numbers nothing—the method notes say so, and citations of the site should name it as the source of the numbering. On this grid rest the three research instruments: a concordance that searches every shipped text at once, so that a term like *reckoning*, *machine*, or *will* can be followed across three millennia in seconds; the Atlas, a co-occurrence network of the corpus’s leading content terms, computed by an open script, in which every node resolves back to citable paragraphs; and a citation-bound dialogue, in which a retrieval running in the reader’s browser selects the paragraphs bearing on a question, and a language model is required to answer from those passages alone, with the canonical citation attached to every claim—the apparatus’s practical answer to the pact described in its coda. The Atlas is offered as a finding aid, not a semantic claim; the dialogue’s answers are reconstructions, to be verified against the editions before use.

The limits are stated as plainly as the method. These are selections chosen for the AI-prehistory argument, not complete works: *Leviathan* is present in its Introduction and first five chapters, not its politics; Boole’s symbolic detail is deliberately thinned in favor of his philosophical frame; the mathematical tables of Lovelace’s Notes, defeated by the surviving scans, are marked as omitted rather than silently reconstructed. Residual transcription errors are possible, and corrections are welcome through the repository. The apparatus, in short, aspires to be trustworthy rather than exhaustive—a place where a reader can verify a quotation, not a substitute for the printed editions it points to.

The recurring discovery of this corpus is that our newest arguments are our oldest. When a contemporary critic objects that a language model merely rearranges what it was given, the objection is Lovelace’s, and Turing’s reply to her is still the reply in use. When an enthusiast declares that fluent conversation settles the question of machine intelligence, Descartes’s test—and his reasons for thinking no machine would pass it—are the proper starting point. When a philosopher insists that whatever the system does, there is no one home, the walk through Leibniz’s mill has already been taken. This is not an argument for deference to the dead; it is an argument for precision. The predecessors did not merely anticipate our questions—they often posed them more carefully than we do, because they posed them without the distraction of a machine that almost works.

The site’s name is therefore also its method. Leibniz’s *Calculemus* was a proposal for how disagreement should end: not in rhetoric, but in a shared procedure that either party can check. A corpus with exact citation is the philological version of the same proposal. The texts are here, whole where they can be, numbered where they are, searchable throughout. When disputes arise about what the tradition actually said—let us calculate.
